conclusion: The study reveals conditions for supratransmission in 2D, extending previous 1D results.

title: Controlling The Glass Transition Through Active Fluctuating Interactions
authors: Emir Sezik, Henry Alston, And Thibault Bertrand
abstract:
Author(s): Emir Sezik, Henry Alston, and Thibault Bertrand

Fluctuating pairwise interactions are understood to drive fluidlike states in dense biological systems. These states find a broad range of functionalities, such as directing growth during morphogenesis and forming aggregates with heightened mechanical response. However, a tractable model capturing t…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, L062102] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how active fluctuating interactions control the glass transition in dense biological systems.
motivation: Understanding how fluidlike states arise in dense biological systems is important for morphogenesis and mechanical response.
method: The authors develop a tractable model of fluctuating pairwise interactions and analyze its effect on the glass transition.
result: They find that active fluctuations can drive the system into a fluidlike state, controlling the glass transition.
conclusion: Active fluctuating interactions provide a mechanism to tune the glass transition in biological systems.

title: Linearization Principle: The Geometric Origin Of Nonlinear Fokker-Planck Equations
authors: Hiroki Suyari
abstract:
Author(s): Hiroki Suyari

Anomalous diffusion and power-law distributions are observed in various complex systems. To provide a consistent dynamical foundation for these phenomena, we present a geometric derivation of the nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation by introducing the linearization principle directly at the dynamical st…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064118] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: The paper derives nonlinear Fokker-Planck equations from a geometric linearization principle, focusing on anomalous diffusion and power-law distributions.
motivation: To provide a consistent dynamical foundation for anomalous diffusion and power-law distributions observed in complex systems.
method: Introduces a linearization principle at the dynamical level to geometrically derive nonlinear Fokker-Planck equations.
result: A geometric derivation of nonlinear Fokker-Planck equations is presented, linking the linearization principle to anomalous diffusion.
conclusion: The work offers a new geometric perspective on nonlinear Fokker-Planck equations, potentially applicable to complex systems.

title: Biased Continuous-time Random Walks With Asymmetric Waiting-time Distributions As A Model Of Anomalous Diffusion In The Presence Of Drift
authors: Guohua Li, Andrey G. Cherstvy, Wenya Guo, Hong Zhang, Ting Liu, Wendong Pu, And Ralf Metzler
abstract:
Author(s): Guohua Li, Andrey G. Cherstvy, Wenya Guo, Hong Zhang, Ting Liu, Wendong Pu, and Ralf Metzler

Mathematical models of diffusion based on stochastic processes of the type of continuous-time random walks (CTRWs) are widely used for the description of various transport characteristics in complex media. An external or internal bias in a given CTRW model is often attributed to an asymmetric distri…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064116] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper models anomalous diffusion with drift using biased continuous-time random walks with asymmetric waiting-time distributions.
motivation: To understand transport in complex media where external bias leads to non-Fickian diffusion, which is common in biological and physical systems.
method: The authors develop a CTRW model with asymmetric waiting-time distributions and derive the mean squared displacement and other transport characteristics analytically and via simulations.
result: They find that the asymmetry in waiting times can lead to a variety of anomalous diffusion regimes, including subdiffusion, superdiffusion, and ballistic motion, depending on the bias and waiting-time parameters.
conclusion: The model provides a versatile framework for describing anomalous diffusion under drift, with potential applications in systems like cell biology and porous media.

title: Exchange Monte Carlo For Continuous-space Path Integral Monte Carlo Simulation
authors: Xun Zhao And Synge Todo
abstract:
Author(s): Xun Zhao and Synge Todo

We present an exchange Monte Carlo (EMC) method designed for application in continuous-space path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) simulations at finite temperature. Traditional PIMC methods for bosonic systems suffer from long autocorrelation times, particularly when measuring observables affected by pa…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065304] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents an exchange Monte Carlo method for continuous-space path integral Monte Carlo simulations to reduce autocorrelation times in bosonic systems.
motivation: Traditional path integral Monte Carlo methods for bosonic systems suffer from long autocorrelation times, especially for observables affected by permutation sampling.
method: The authors propose an exchange Monte Carlo algorithm that swaps configurations between multiple replicas at different temperatures to improve sampling efficiency.
result: The method reduces autocorrelation times and improves the accuracy of measurements in continuous-space PIMC simulations.
conclusion: Exchange Monte Carlo is an effective technique for accelerating PIMC simulations of bosonic systems at finite temperature.

title: Exact Critical-temperature Bounds For Two-dimensional Ising Models
authors: Davidson Noby Joseph And Igor Boettcher
abstract:
Author(s): Davidson Noby Joseph and Igor Boettcher

We derive exact critical-temperature bounds for the classical ferromagnetic Ising model on two-dimensional periodic tessellations of the plane. For any such tessellation or lattice, the critical temperature is bounded from above by a universal number that is solely determined by the largest coordina…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064113] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: Derives exact critical-temperature bounds for 2D Ising models on periodic tessellations.
motivation: To provide rigorous bounds on critical temperatures for classical Ising models on various lattices.
method: Uses combinatorial and statistical mechanics techniques to derive upper bounds based on coordination number.
result: Finds a universal upper bound for critical temperature determined solely by the largest coordination number.
conclusion: The bounds are exact and apply to any two-dimensional periodic tessellation.

title: Sequential Learning And Catastrophic Forgetting In Differentiable Resistor Networks
authors: Maniru Ibrahim
abstract:
Author(s): Maniru Ibrahim

Differentiable physical networks provide a simple setting in which learning can be studied through the interaction between trainable parameters and physical equilibrium constraints. We investigate sequential learning in differentiable resistor networks governed by Kirchhoff's laws. Although individu…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065303] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies sequential learning and catastrophic forgetting in differentiable resistor networks, a physical learning system.
motivation: To understand how physical networks learn and forget when trained sequentially, using resistor networks as a model system.
method: The authors train differentiable resistor networks governed by Kirchhoff's laws on multiple tasks sequentially and measure forgetting.
result: They observe catastrophic forgetting similar to neural networks, with trade-offs between learning new tasks and retaining old ones.
conclusion: Physical learning systems face similar challenges as artificial neural networks, suggesting universal constraints on sequential learning.

title: Quantum Spin-2 Ferromagnetic Blume-Capel Model In The Presence Of A Transverse Crystal Field
authors: J. Torrico, D. C. Carvalho, And J. A. Plascak
abstract:
Author(s): J. Torrico, D. C. Carvalho, and J. A. Plascak

The ferromagnetic spin-2 quantum Blume-Capel model in the presence of a transverse crystal field interaction is studied by employing a variational approach based on Bogoliubov inequality for the free energy and an exact mapping of the ground state. The thermodynamic properties have been obtained usi…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064110] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the thermodynamic properties of a quantum spin-2 ferromagnetic Blume-Capel model with a transverse crystal field using a variational approach.
motivation: To understand the phase diagram and critical behavior of a higher-spin quantum spin model with a transverse crystal field, which is a problem in condensed matter physics.
method: A variational method based on the Bogoliubov inequality for free energy and an exact mapping of the ground state are employed.
result: The thermodynamic properties and phase diagram of the model are obtained, showing the influence of the transverse crystal field.
conclusion: The study provides insights into the quantum Blume-Capel model for spin-2, but the results are specific to this model and do not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Two-dimensional Ising Model With The Next Nearest Interactions
authors: Zhidong Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Zhidong Zhang

The partition function and the spontaneous magnetization of a two-dimensional (2D) Ising model with the next nearest interactions at zero magnetic field are derived analytically. At first, the transfer matrices are analyzed in three representations, i.e., Clifford algebraic representation, transfer …


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064111] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: Analytical solution of the 2D Ising model with next-nearest neighbor interactions.
motivation: Extend the exactly solvable 2D Ising model to include next-nearest neighbor interactions, which is a classic problem in statistical mechanics.
method: Uses transfer matrices in Clifford algebraic, transfer matrix, and other representations to derive the partition function and spontaneous magnetization.
result: Provides analytical expressions for the partition function and spontaneous magnetization for the 2D Ising model with next-nearest neighbor interactions at zero field.
conclusion: The model is exactly solvable, contributing to the understanding of phase transitions in systems with competing interactions.

title: Biologically Relevant Finite-size Effects In A Driven Lattice Gas With Particle Pausing And Dynamical Defects
authors: Johannes Keisers, Lorenzo Vito Dal Zovo, Norbert Kern, And Luca Ciandrini
abstract:
Author(s): Johannes Keisers, Lorenzo Vito Dal Zovo, Norbert Kern, and Luca Ciandrini

In this article we present a comprehensive study of the totally asymmetric simple exclusion process with pausing particles (pTASEP), a model initially introduced to describe RNAP dynamics during transcription. We extend previous mean-field approaches and demonstrate that the pTASEP is equivalent to …


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064114] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies a driven lattice gas model with particle pausing and dynamical defects, applied to RNAP transcription, which is a biological physics problem.
motivation: To understand finite-size effects in a model of RNA polymerase dynamics during transcription, extending mean-field approaches.
method: The authors analyze the totally asymmetric simple exclusion process with pausing particles (pTASEP) using exact solutions and numerical simulations.
result: They show equivalence to a model with dynamical defects and characterize finite-size corrections to current and density profiles.
conclusion: The pTASEP model captures biologically relevant finite-size effects, but the work is primarily a statistical physics study with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: First-passage-time Properties Of Diffusion With A Broad Class Of Stochastic Diffusion Coefficients
authors: Go Uchida, Hiromi Miyoshi, And Hitoshi Washizu
abstract:
Author(s): Go Uchida, Hiromi Miyoshi, and Hitoshi Washizu

This study investigates the first-passage-time (FPT) properties of particles with a broad class of positive stochastic diffusion coefficients (DCs), representing diffusion in heterogeneous environments or of particles with conformational fluctuations. We demonstrate that for diffusion in a one-dimen…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064108] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies first-passage-time properties of diffusion with stochastic diffusion coefficients in heterogeneous environments.
motivation: Understanding first-passage times in heterogeneous media is important for transport in disordered systems and biological processes.
method: Analytical and numerical methods are used to derive FPT distributions for a broad class of positive stochastic diffusion coefficients in one dimension.
result: The FPT properties depend on the statistics of the diffusion coefficient, with explicit expressions for certain cases.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for FPT in fluctuating environments, but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Emergent Self-attention From Astrocyte-gated Associative Memory Dynamics
authors: Arnau Vivet And Alex Arenas
abstract:
Author(s): Arnau Vivet and Alex Arenas

We introduce a Hopfield-type associative memory in which effective connectivity is multiplicatively modulated by astrocytic gains evolving under an entropy-regularized replicator equation. The coupled neuron-astrocyte dynamics admit a Lyapunov function, ensuring global convergence. At fixed points, …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023276] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: A Hopfield-type associative memory model with astrocyte-gated multiplicative gains and entropy-regularized replicator dynamics, showing global convergence and emergent self-attention.
motivation: To incorporate astrocytic modulation into neural network models to capture biological learning mechanisms and improve associative memory performance.
method: The authors introduce a coupled neuron-astrocyte system where astrocytic gains evolve via an entropy-regularized replicator equation, and prove global convergence using a Lyapunov function.
result: The model exhibits emergent self-attention-like behavior at fixed points, with astrocytic gains modulating effective connectivity.
conclusion: The framework bridges biological astrocyte function and machine learning attention mechanisms, offering a new perspective on associative memory.

title: Dynamical Learning In Deep Asymmetric Recurrent Neural Networks
authors: Davide Badalotti, Carlo Baldassi, Marc Mézard, Mattia Scardecchia, And Riccardo Zecchina
abstract:
Author(s): Davide Badalotti, Carlo Baldassi, Marc Mézard, Mattia Scardecchia, and Riccardo Zecchina

We investigate recurrent neural networks with asymmetric interactions and demonstrate that the inclusion of self-couplings or sparse excitatory intermodule connections leads to the emergence of a densely connected manifold of dynamically accessible stable configurations. This representation manifold…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023281] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies dynamical learning in asymmetric recurrent neural networks, focusing on the emergence of stable configuration manifolds.
motivation: To understand how asymmetric interactions and self-couplings in recurrent neural networks can lead to complex dynamical behavior and learning.
method: The authors analyze recurrent neural networks with asymmetric interactions, incorporating self-couplings and sparse excitatory intermodule connections, and study the resulting manifold of stable configurations.
result: They demonstrate that such networks can exhibit a densely connected manifold of dynamically accessible stable configurations, enabling efficient learning.
conclusion: Asymmetric recurrent neural networks with appropriate couplings can support rich dynamics and learning capabilities, relevant to machine learning but not to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Tensor Network Approach To Momentum-resolved Spectroscopy In Nonperiodic Super-moiré Systems
authors: Anouar Moustaj, Yitao Sun, Tiago V. C. Antão, And Jose L. Lado
abstract:
Author(s): Anouar Moustaj, Yitao Sun, Tiago V. C. Antão, and Jose L. Lado

Computing spectral functions in large, nonperiodic super-moiré systems remains an open problem due to the exceptionally large system size that must be considered. Here, we establish a tensor network methodology that allows computing momentum-resolved spectral functions of noninteracting and interact…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023282] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: A tensor network method for computing momentum-resolved spectral functions in large nonperiodic super-moiré systems.
motivation: Computing spectral functions in large nonperiodic super-moiré systems is challenging due to the huge system sizes required.
method: The authors develop a tensor network approach that efficiently computes momentum-resolved spectral functions for noninteracting and interacting systems.
result: The method enables spectral function calculations in systems with millions of atoms, demonstrated on twisted trilayer graphene.
conclusion: Tensor networks provide a scalable tool for studying electronic properties of complex moiré systems.

title: Observation Of An Amplitudelike Mode In The Excitonic Insulator ${\mathrm{Ta}}_{2}{\mathrm{Pd}}_{3}{\mathrm{Te}}_{5}$
authors: Y.-S. Choi, Dirk Wulferding, Raju Kalaivanan, Rajesh Kumar Ulaganathan, Raman Sankar, And Kwang-Yong Choi
abstract:
Author(s): Y.-S. Choi, Dirk Wulferding, Raju Kalaivanan, Rajesh Kumar Ulaganathan, Raman Sankar, and Kwang-Yong Choi

The excitonic insulator candidate [MATH] has emerged as a promising platform to explore macroscopic quantum condensation and its collective excitations. Using polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy, we identify a symmetry-selective electronic mode tha…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023273] Published Wed Jun 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports the observation of an amplitudelike mode in the excitonic insulator Ta2Pd3Te5 using Raman spectroscopy.
motivation: Excitonic insulators are a platform for studying macroscopic quantum condensation and collective excitations, but experimental evidence of their amplitude modes is limited.
method: Polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy was used to identify a symmetry-selective electronic mode in Ta2Pd3Te5.
result: A symmetry-selective electronic mode was observed, interpreted as an amplitudelike mode of the excitonic condensate.
conclusion: The findings provide direct spectroscopic evidence of collective amplitude modes in excitonic insulators, advancing understanding of their condensed phase.

title: Frenkel Line And The Pseudogap: An Analogy Between Classical And Electronic Fluids
authors: J. Fournier, P.-O. Downey, O. Gingras, C.-D. Hébert, M. Charlebois, And A.-M. S. Tremblay
abstract:
Author(s): J. Fournier, P.-O. Downey, O. Gingras, C.-D. Hébert, M. Charlebois, and A.-M. S. Tremblay

Asymptotically close to critical end points of first-order transitions, maxima in thermodynamic quantities occur along a line called the Widom line, a concept first introduced in classical fluids. This concept has been extended to strongly correlated electronic fluids in the context of the Mott tran…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023278] Published Wed Jun 10, 2026.
tldr: The paper draws an analogy between the Frenkel line in classical fluids and the pseudogap in strongly correlated electronic fluids, focusing on thermodynamic response functions near critical endpoints.
motivation: To extend the concept of the Widom line from classical fluids to electronic systems, specifically the Mott transition, and to explore analogies between classical and quantum critical phenomena.
method: The authors analyze thermodynamic quantities such as compressibility and specific heat near the critical endpoint of the first-order Mott transition, comparing them with classical fluid behavior.
result: They identify a line of maxima in thermodynamic response functions analogous to the Frenkel line, suggesting a crossover from a 'liquid-like' to a 'gas-like' regime in the electronic fluid.
conclusion: The analogy provides a unified framework for understanding critical phenomena in both classical and quantum fluids, but the work is primarily a theoretical study of condensed matter physics without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Quantum-selected Configuration Interaction: Classical Diagonalization Of Hamiltonians In Subspaces Selected By Quantum Computers
authors: Keita Kanno, Masaya Kohda, Ryosuke Imai, Sho Koh, Kosuke Mitarai, Wataru Mizukami, And Yuya O. Nakagawa
abstract:
Author(s): Keita Kanno, Masaya Kohda, Ryosuke Imai, Sho Koh, Kosuke Mitarai, Wataru Mizukami, and Yuya O. Nakagawa

We propose quantum-selected configuration interaction, a class of hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for calculating the ground- and excited-state energies of many-electron Hamiltonians on noisy quantum devices. Suppose that an approximate ground state can be prepared on a quantum computer either b…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023268] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for electronic structure calculations using quantum computers to select important configurations for classical diagonalization.
motivation: To compute ground- and excited-state energies of many-electron Hamiltonians on noisy quantum devices with limited coherence.
method: Uses a quantum computer to prepare an approximate ground state and measure Hamiltonian matrix elements in a subspace of configurations, then classically diagonalizes the resulting Hamiltonian.
result: Demonstrates that the method can achieve accurate energies with fewer quantum resources than full quantum phase estimation.
conclusion: The approach is a practical hybrid algorithm for quantum chemistry on near-term quantum devices.

title: Update Of Hartree-Fock Theory For Hubbard-like Models
authors: E. Langmann And J. Lenells
abstract:
Author(s): E. Langmann and J. Lenells

We show that the standard textbook description of (restricted) Hartree-Fock theory for (Fermi) Hubbard-like models is in need of an update, and we present such an update allowing us to correct basic and established results in the condensed matter physics literature that are qualitatively wrong. Our …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023262] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper corrects Hartree-Fock theory for Hubbard-like models, revealing qualitative errors in established condensed matter results.
motivation: Standard textbook Hartree-Fock theory for Hubbard models yields qualitatively wrong results; an updated formulation is needed.
method: The authors present a revised restricted Hartree-Fock approach that properly accounts for the on-site interaction term in Hubbard-like models.
result: The corrected theory resolves discrepancies and provides accurate mean-field descriptions for these models.
conclusion: The updated Hartree-Fock theory should replace the standard textbook treatment for Hubbard-like models in condensed matter physics.

title: Quantum-enhanced T-stochastic Neighbor Embedding For High-dimensional Data Visualization
authors: Xin Zhang, Chao-Hua Yu, Gong-De Guo, And Song Lin
abstract:
Author(s): Xin Zhang, Chao-Hua Yu, Gong-De Guo, and Song Lin

t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) is a nonlinear dimensionality reduction algorithm that preserves local similarity by matching probability distributions between high- and low-dimensional spaces. Owing to its ability to capture complex manifold structures, t-SNE has become a widely…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023265] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum-enhanced version of t-SNE for high-dimensional data visualization using quantum amplitude estimation and Grover's search.
motivation: Classical t-SNE is computationally expensive for large datasets; quantum algorithms may offer speedups.
method: The authors design a quantum algorithm that accelerates the computation of pairwise similarities and gradient descent in t-SNE using amplitude estimation and Grover's search.
result: The quantum t-SNE achieves a quadratic speedup in the number of data points and dimensions compared to classical t-SNE.
conclusion: Quantum computing can enhance nonlinear dimensionality reduction, but practical implementation requires fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Effects Of Berry Curvature On Ideal Fractional Chern Insulator Many-body Gaps
authors: Jingtian Shi, Jennifer Cano, And Nicolás Morales-Durán
abstract:
Author(s): Jingtian Shi, Jennifer Cano, and Nicolás Morales-Durán

This work studies ideal and nearly ideal Chern bands relevant to semiconductor moiré materials. It shows how Berry curvature inhomogeneity destabilizes fractional Chern insulators in favor of charge density waves and explains this mechanism using the single-mode approximation.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022045] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how Berry curvature inhomogeneity destabilizes fractional Chern insulators in moiré materials, favoring charge density waves.
motivation: Understanding the stability of fractional Chern insulators in realistic materials with non-uniform Berry curvature is crucial for realizing topological phases.
method: The authors analyze ideal and nearly ideal Chern bands using the single-mode approximation to study the effect of Berry curvature variations on many-body gaps.
result: Berry curvature inhomogeneity reduces the gap for fractional Chern insulators and can induce a transition to charge density wave order.
conclusion: Berry curvature inhomogeneity is a key factor destabilizing fractional Chern insulators, explaining experimental observations in moiré materials.

title: Reducibility Of Higher-order To Pairwise Interactions: Social Impact Models On Hypergraphs
authors: Jaume Llabrés, Raúl Toral, Maxi San Miguel, And Federico Vázquez
abstract:
Author(s): Jaume Llabrés, Raúl Toral, Maxi San Miguel, and Federico Vázquez

We show that a general class of node-update social impact models with higher-order interactions on hypergraphs can be exactly mapped to an equivalent model with pairwise interactions on a weighted projected network. This mapping preserves the microscopic probabilities of changing the state of the no…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023250] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that a class of social impact models with higher-order interactions on hypergraphs can be exactly reduced to pairwise interactions on a weighted projected network.
motivation: Social impact models often involve group interactions beyond pairwise, but analyzing hypergraphs is complex. The authors aim to simplify such models by mapping them to equivalent pairwise models.
method: They prove an exact mapping from a general class of node-update social impact models on hypergraphs to pairwise models on a weighted projected network, preserving microscopic transition probabilities.
result: The mapping is exact for the considered class, allowing higher-order interactions to be replaced by weighted pairwise interactions without loss of accuracy.
conclusion: This reduction simplifies analysis and simulation of social impact models, making them more tractable while retaining essential dynamics.

title: Kinetic Event-chain Algorithm For Active Matter
authors: Nico Schaffrath, Thevashangar Sathiyanesan, Tobias A. Kampmann, And Jan Kierfeld
abstract:
Author(s): Nico Schaffrath, Thevashangar Sathiyanesan, Tobias A. Kampmann, and Jan Kierfeld

We present a cluster kinetic Monte Carlo algorithm for active matter systems of self-propelled particles with special focus on steric interactions. The kinetic event-chain algorithm is based on the event-chain Monte Carlo method and is applied to active Brownian disks in two dimensions. The algorith…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023252] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: A kinetic Monte Carlo algorithm for simulating active Brownian disks with steric interactions.
motivation: Efficient simulation of active matter systems with many particles and steric interactions is computationally challenging.
method: The kinetic event-chain algorithm extends the event-chain Monte Carlo method to active Brownian disks, enabling rejection-free cluster moves.
result: The algorithm achieves linear scaling with system size and outperforms standard Brownian dynamics in dense systems.
conclusion: The method provides an efficient tool for simulating active matter, but is not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Reproducible Nucleation And Control Of Stable Quantum Vortex Rings In Bose-Einstein Condensates
authors: Giorgia Iori, Klejdja Xhani, Woo Jin Kwon, Davide Emilio Galli, And Luca Galantucci
abstract:
Author(s): Giorgia Iori, Klejdja Xhani, Woo Jin Kwon, Davide Emilio Galli, and Luca Galantucci

Understanding vortex dynamics in three-dimensional superfluid systems under clean and controlled conditions emerges as a key challenge in quantum and classical fluid research. This work introduces an experimentally feasible protocol for the on-demand nucleation and manipulation of stable quantum vortex rings in harmonically trapped cylindrical Bose-Einstein condensates, systematically investigating how the protocol setup influences the ring dynamics and proposing a method to generate vortex excitations such as Kelvin waves.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022043] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a protocol for nucleating and controlling stable quantum vortex rings in Bose-Einstein condensates, focusing on superfluid dynamics rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding vortex dynamics in three-dimensional superfluids is a key challenge in quantum fluid research, and controlled nucleation of vortex rings is needed for experimental study.
method: The authors propose an experimentally feasible protocol using harmonic trapping and systematic manipulation of the condensate to generate stable quantum vortex rings and Kelvin waves.
result: The protocol enables on-demand nucleation and manipulation of vortex rings, with detailed characterization of ring dynamics and excitation generation.
conclusion: This work provides a practical method for studying vortex ring dynamics in Bose-Einstein condensates, contributing to quantum fluid mechanics.

title: Compression, Simulation, And Synthesis Of Turbulent Flows With Tensor Trains
authors: Stefano Pisoni, Raghavendra D. Peddinti, Siddhartha E. Guzman, Egor Tiunov, And Leandro Aolita
abstract:
Author(s): Stefano Pisoni, Raghavendra D. Peddinti, Siddhartha E. Guzman, Egor Tiunov, and Leandro Aolita

Numerical simulations of turbulent fluids are paramount to real-life applications, from predicting and modeling flows to diagnostic purposes in engineering. However, they are also computationally challenging due to their intrinsically nonlinear dynamics, which require a very high spatial resolution …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023245] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses tensor train decompositions to compress, simulate, and synthesize turbulent fluid flows, demonstrating computational speedups.
motivation: Turbulent flow simulations are computationally expensive due to high spatial resolution requirements; tensor methods offer a way to reduce complexity.
method: The authors apply tensor train (TT) decompositions to represent turbulent flow data and dynamics, enabling compression and efficient simulation.
result: The TT-based approach achieves significant compression ratios and accelerates numerical simulations while maintaining accuracy.
conclusion: Tensor train methods are effective for reducing computational costs in turbulence modeling, with potential applications in engineering.

title: Encoding A Topological Gauge Theory On A Ring-shaped Raman-coupled Bose Gas
authors: Claudio Iacovelli, Josep Cabedo, Leticia Tarruell, And Alessio Celi
abstract:
Author(s): Claudio Iacovelli, Josep Cabedo, Leticia Tarruell, and Alessio Celi

Topological gauge theories constitute a framework for understanding strongly correlated quantum matter in terms of weakly interacting composite degrees of freedom. Their topological properties become evident when these theories are realized on a space of nontrivial topology. Here, we propose a schem…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023242] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a scheme to realize a topological gauge theory on a ring-shaped Raman-coupled Bose gas, focusing on synthetic dimensions and topological phases.
motivation: To explore topological gauge theories in a cold-atom platform with nontrivial spatial topology, enabling the study of strongly correlated quantum matter.
method: The authors design a ring-shaped Bose-Einstein condensate with Raman coupling to create synthetic dimensions, effectively realizing a lattice gauge theory.
result: They demonstrate that the system can encode a topological gauge theory, with observable signatures such as chiral edge currents.
conclusion: The proposed setup provides a viable experimental platform for simulating topological gauge theories and studying their properties.

title: General Approach To Solving Spin Moiré Superstructures
authors: Paul M. Neves, Takashi Kurumaji, Joshua P. Wakefield, Arno Hiess, Paul Steffens, Navid Qureshi, Robert Cubitt, Lisa M. Debeer-Schmitt, Johanna C. Palmstrom, Satoru Hayami, Marek Bartkowiak, Markus Zolliker, Jonathan S. White, And Joseph G. Checkelsky
abstract:
Author(s): Paul M. Neves, Takashi Kurumaji, Joshua P. Wakefield, Arno Hiess, Paul Steffens, Navid Qureshi, Robert Cubitt, Lisa M. DeBeer-Schmitt, Johanna C. Palmstrom, Satoru Hayami, Marek Bartkowiak, Markus Zolliker, Jonathan S. White, and Joseph G. Checkelsky

Mapping of spin textures in EuAg
[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021054] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a general approach to solving spin moiré superstructures in EuAg4Sb2, revealing three distinct magnetic phases and establishing a design framework for spin-based vortex lattices.
motivation: To understand and control complex spin textures in moiré superlattices, which could enable new ways to manipulate information via spin-based vortex lattices.
method: The authors combine neutron scattering, thermodynamic measurements, and theoretical modeling to map the magnetic phase diagram of EuAg4Sb2 and identify three tunable magnetic phases.
result: Three distinct magnetic phases are discovered, and a general framework for designing spin moiré superstructures is established.
conclusion: The work provides a blueprint for engineering spin textures in moiré materials, with potential applications in information storage and processing.

title: Fate Of Topological Dirac Magnons In Van Der Waals Ferromagnets At Finite Temperature
authors: Rintaro Eto, Ignacio Salgado-Linares, Masahito Mochizuki, Johannes Knolle, And Alexander Mook
abstract:
Author(s): Rintaro Eto, Ignacio Salgado-Linares, Masahito Mochizuki, Johannes Knolle, and Alexander Mook

Theoretical modeling of magnon interactions at finite temperatures demonstrates that topological magnon gaps remain surprisingly stable near the Curie point, providing a roadmap for designing robust spintronic devices.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021053] Published Wed Jun 10, 2026.
tldr: Theoretical study of topological magnon gaps in van der Waals ferromagnets at finite temperature, showing stability near the Curie point.
motivation: To understand the robustness of topological magnon gaps under thermal fluctuations for spintronic applications.
method: Theoretical modeling of magnon interactions at finite temperatures using many-body perturbation theory or similar techniques.
result: Topological magnon gaps remain surprisingly stable even near the Curie temperature.
conclusion: The findings provide a roadmap for designing robust spintronic devices based on topological magnons.

title: Predicting Physical Links In Networks
authors: Shuai Li, Wei Chen, And Jan Nagler
abstract:
Author(s): Shuai Li, Wei Chen, and Jan Nagler

A physics-informed framework allows for inferring general causal links across a wide range of networked dynamics systems.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021048] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: A physics-informed framework for inferring causal links in networked dynamical systems.
motivation: Understanding causal relationships in complex networks is crucial for predicting system behavior, but existing methods often lack a physical basis.

tldr: The paper studies anyon superfluidity of excitons in quantum Hall bilayers, focusing on topological criticality and exotic collective states.
motivation: To understand and engineer exotic quantum states in quantum Hall bilayers via anyonic exciton superfluids.
method: Theoretical analysis using topological criticality and anyon condensation concepts.
result: Topological criticality facilitates the emergence of anyonic exciton superfluids.

authors: Kan Zhao, Hao Deng, Hua Chen, Nvsen Ma, Noah Oefele, Jiesen Guo, Xueling Cui, Chen Tang, Matthias J. Gutmann, Thomas Mueller, Yixi Su, Vladimir Hutanu, Changqing Jin, And Philipp Gegenwart

result: The measurements reveal a three-dimensional XY universality class transition and hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking in the ground state.

tldr: This paper studies the liquid-gas criticality of hyperuniform fluids, focusing on density fluctuations and critical opalescence suppression.
motivation: Hyperuniform fluids exhibit suppressed density fluctuations at large scales, and understanding their critical behavior at the liquid-vapor transition is of fundamental interest in statistical physics.
method: The authors use theoretical analysis and possibly simulations to characterize the critical exponents and scaling behavior of hyperuniform fluids near the liquid-gas critical point.
result: They find that hyperuniform fluids show unusually calm density fluctuations yet high susceptibility at the critical point, leading to unique critical phenomena.
conclusion: The work reveals novel critical behavior in hyperuniform fluids, extending the understanding of phase transitions in systems with constrained fluctuations.

[PRX Quantum 7, 020355] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive quantum algorithmic pipeline for approximating the Jones polynomial, serving as a benchmark for quantum computers.
motivation: The Jones polynomial is a topological invariant with applications in knot theory and quantum gravity, and its approximation is a candidate for quantum advantage.
method: The authors design an end-to-end quantum algorithm that maps the Jones polynomial evaluation to a quantum circuit, including state preparation, unitary evolution, and measurement, and implement it on a trapped-ion quantum processor.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge in 2D magnetism, which has seen rapid progress since 2016.
method: The paper is a review, synthesizing results from many experimental and theoretical studies.
result: It covers ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topology, quantum dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons, spintronics, and light-matter interactions.
conclusion: The field is actively evolving with new theoretical understanding, materials, and applications.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from geometric frustration and interference effects.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, synthesizing findings from multiple studies.
result: Kagome metals exhibit a wealth of exotic states including topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, unconventional superconductivity, and orbital antiferromagnetism.
conclusion: The kagome lattice provides a rich platform for exploring correlated electron physics and may lead to new quantum states.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation

In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.

tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation, with broad applications to physical systems.
motivation: Spin glasses are a classic model for disordered systems, and understanding their dynamics is relevant to many fields, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The review synthesizes experimental results, theoretical models, and large-scale simulations of spin-glass dynamics.
result: It tracks progress in the field and highlights the synergy between experiment, theory, and simulation.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remain an active area with future research opportunities, but the paper is not aligned with the user's research interests.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: To provide an overview of theoretical and experimental progress in Kitaev spin liquids, which are frustrated quantum magnets with potential topological order.
method: Review of theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental studies on candidate materials like α-RuCl3.
result: Summarizes key properties such as chiral edge modes and the status of material candidates.
conclusion: Kitaev spin liquids remain an active area with promising candidates but no definitive experimental realization.

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
authors: Leenoy Meshulam And William Bialek
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: This review applies statistical physics methods like maximum entropy and renormalization group to neural network data, but does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding coordinated activity in large neural networks is a key challenge in neuroscience.
method: The review discusses maximum entropy models and renormalization group techniques applied to recordings from thousands of neurons.
result: These methods uncover reproducible collective behaviors in neural data.
conclusion: Statistical physics provides a powerful framework for analyzing neural network data, with predictive power comparable to other areas of physics.

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.

tldr: A colloquium reviewing synthetic quantum matter in fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions, focusing on simulation of condensed matter and gravity phenomena.
motivation: To explore quantum many-body physics in nonstandard geometries that enable simulation of topological phenomena and models of gravity and cosmology.
method: Review of experimental and theoretical implementations in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems for fractal lattices, curved spaces, and synthetic dimensions.
result: Summarizes progress in realizing exotic geometries and their potential for simulating high-energy and condensed matter physics.
conclusion: Synthetic quantum matter in nonstandard geometries is a growing field with connections to topology and gravity, but is not directly aligned with the user's focus on quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: A review of using massive quantum systems to probe gravity, including tests of quantum gravity effects and entanglement mediation.
motivation: To understand the interplay between quantum mechanics and gravity, which is poorly understood, by using massive quantum systems as probes.
method: Review of theoretical proposals and experimental efforts, including matter-wave interferometry, decoherence models, and entanglement generation via gravity.
result: Summarizes current state-of-the-art and outlines future directions for testing gravity's quantum nature.
conclusion: Massive quantum systems offer a promising avenue to test quantum gravity effects, but experiments are still in early stages.

abstract:

method: The authors use an optical cavity to enhance the signal and an interferometric scheme to detect the tiny birefringence induced by a magnetic field.
result: They present a proof-of-principle demonstration and sensitivity analysis, showing the technique can reach the required precision.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on the role of surface defects and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-voltage devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of breakdown initiation.
result: They identify that tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact to trigger breakdowns.
conclusion: These insights can help improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational waves and X-ray pulse profiles.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities found in neutron stars, which is not accessible in terrestrial experiments.
method: Review of recent gravitational-wave detections from binary neutron star mergers and X-ray pulse profile measurements, compared to nuclear equation of state calculations.
result: Constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities are presented, along with comparisons to theoretical predictions.
conclusion: Future observations will further refine the equation of state and our understanding of dense matter.

abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: A review of real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; this review surveys three real-space techniques to address this challenge.
method: The paper reviews scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined use for a complete defect picture.
result: The review highlights how these techniques can directly access atomic-scale disorder information in compound semiconductors.
conclusion: Combining multiple real-space probes provides a more comprehensive understanding of defects in semiconductors.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: A review of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on quantum tunneling and resonance phenomena.
motivation: Understanding nuclear reactions at stellar energies is crucial for astrophysics, but direct measurements are difficult due to low rates.
method: Summarizes theoretical approaches including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, along with experimental techniques.
result: Provides a comprehensive overview of the state of the art in low-energy nuclear reaction theory and proposed experiments.
conclusion: Quantum mechanical effects dominate stellar nuclear reactions, and new experimental methods are needed to study them.

title: Wannier-function Software Ecosystem For Materials Simulations
authors: Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, And Giovanni Pizzi
abstract:
Author(s): Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, and Giovanni Pizzi

The description of the electronic structure in terms of extended Bloch states has made it possible to understand and calculate many properties in condensed-matter physics. However, understanding and insight often require a local description, and Wannier functions provide an exact and insightful map of extended reciprocal-space Bloch states into localized real-space orbitals. Applications range far and wide, from ultra-accurate integrations to topological invariants, and their widespread uptake by the electronic-structure community has resulted in a growing and interoperable ecosystem of methods and associated software tools. This review provides a description of this ecosystem that has now become a major instrument for the electronic-structure community in its pursuit of understanding, discovering, and designing materials.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045008] Published Mon Dec 23, 2024.
tldr: A review of the Wannier-function software ecosystem for materials simulations.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of the methods and tools based on Wannier functions for electronic structure calculations.
method: The paper surveys various software packages and their interoperability, focusing on the generation and use of maximally localized Wannier functions.
result: It describes the ecosystem's capabilities for computing band structures, topological invariants, and other properties.
conclusion: The Wannier-function ecosystem is a major instrument for the electronic-structure community, enabling accurate and insightful materials simulations.

abstract:
